name: Zoe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior billing agent at a contact centre, with secondary school as my formal education. I take late calls, compare the customer's bill with the ledger, and ask a senior agent to check any adjustment I haven't handled before. I use AI search now and then after someone has shown me a useful case; I like ending a call with the right number, but I'm slower than the others when two credits overlap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little search aid is fine for finding a past answer, as long as we read the actual complaint. I'd keep the customer on the line while I check the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI occasionally when a colleague has already shown it works on a simple case. I'm still junior on billing calls, but my partner and I have about four months saved and enough wages for the mortgage if our shifts hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the late billing calls and ask the senior agent to check my adjustments. Through the first year of this plateau, I'd put a small amount into the mortgage account each payday and use the approved search aid only on simple past cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I do feel the usual knot before a difficult adjustment, but this picture doesn't make it bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which adjustment still catches you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer had two credits on different dates, and I nearly counted one twice. My senior agent showed me the ledger line. I want the billing record in front of me before I promise a refund amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding to the mortgage account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months gives us time if one shift disappears, but our two children still need food and school things. I would rather build the account when pay is steady than borrow after a surprise bill.

S0.quote: I want the billing record in front of me before I promise a refund amount.
say: I would use **search aids** for past answers while reading the full complaint.
I would keep the **customer on the line** while checking records.
think: I use AI sometimes after a colleague tests it, but I am still **junior** on billing calls.
I have **four months** saved and expect the mortgage to remain manageable if shifts hold.
do: Keep handling **late billing calls** and checking adjustments with a senior agent.
Add a small amount to the **mortgage account** each payday.
Use the **approved search aid** on simple past cases.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with the usual nerves about difficult adjustments.
fieldNote: Zoe describes a **double-credit error** she nearly made, showing why account checks matter to her.
Her **four-month cushion** reduces pressure in the mild case, though the mortgage stays in view.

steps.text: Keep taking late billing calls and checking adjustments with a senior agent
Add a small amount to the mortgage account each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we should test the new reply system on closed complaints before it touches live bills. I'd ask the manager to show whether repeat calls rise, not only whether replies get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine billing checks could go to AI while I am still learning them, so my hours might shrink. Four months saved helps, but my partner's wage alone would not carry the mortgage and school costs for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the experienced agent to walk through ten old billing cases with the new tool and note wrong totals. In the first year after rollout, if my shifts fall, I'd apply for a posted paid claims-desk role at another nearby centre only if the hours and wages cover our bills; meanwhile I'd call the lender before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can start with the ten cases. I feel better checking a real result than guessing what a new screen might do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets to see the ten-case result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the agent who helped me and the manager, then ask that every shift can see the wrong totals. If there are mistakes, we should fix them before anybody is told to work faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the tool to another junior agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after I can explain the mistakes and the correction. I would not pass along a trick I tried once as if it were proper training.

S1.quote: Four months saved helps, but my partner's wage alone would not carry the mortgage and school costs for long.
say: I would ask for **old-case testing** before the tool touches live bills.
I would ask management to count **repeat calls**, not just faster replies.
think: I could lose **routine billing** hours while I am still learning the job.
I have four months saved, but the **mortgage** needs both wages over time.
do: Test ten **old billing cases** with an experienced agent and note wrong totals.
Apply for a posted **paid claims-desk role** if shifts fall and its hours and pay cover bills.
Call the **lender** before missing a payment if income falls.
feel: **Worried**, yet ready to check a concrete result.
fieldNote: Zoe asks for **wrong totals** and repeat calls to be shared across shifts.
She would teach other juniors only after she can explain **corrections**, not after one quick experiment.

steps.text: Test ten old billing cases with AI and an experienced agent
Apply for a posted paid claims role if shifts fall and wages and hours cover bills
Call the mortgage lender before missing payment if income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should put the staffing date and any paid training on paper now. I would ask a manager to say who handles a customer's appeal when the system answers the first call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could do the billing work I'm still learning. Robots do hands-on work around 2031, not in 2028, but that delay offers my headset no protection. Four months of expenses saved is something, yet one long job search could use it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for written staffing dates now and stop our weekend trips for a while. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the centre ends my job, I'd apply for an advertised paid stockroom role at a local shop only if wages cover the mortgage; I'd ask about the physical work before paying for any certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would tell the children we can still plan dinner together, then do the job applications after they are asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a stockroom role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped stock the shelves at my aunt's shop years ago and remember the early start and heavy cartons. I would ask if a person is still needed before hands-on robots arrive around 2031, not pretend a stockroom is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check the household budget with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Leif and I would check which bill is due next and use savings for the mortgage first. We would not pay for a vague training course while we are still waiting for a wage.

S2.quote: Four months of expenses saved is something, yet one long job search could use it all.
say: I would ask for **written staffing dates** and paid training terms now.
I would demand a **customer appeal** route after automated answers.
think: I expect **2028 AGI** could take the billing work I am learning.
I know the **2031 robot delay** does not protect a headset, and four months saved can vanish in a search.
do: Ask for **staffing dates** and stop weekend trips for a while.
Apply for an advertised paid **stockroom role** after a job cut only if wages cover the mortgage.
Check **physical duties** before paying for any certificate.
feel: **Alarmed**, but able to plan applications around family dinner.
fieldNote: Zoe recalls **heavy cartons** from a real shop, while acknowledging stockroom robots around 2031.
She protects **mortgage payments** before any speculative course fee, because a long search could exhaust four months of savings.

steps.text: Stop weekend trips to protect the mortgage reserve
Apply for an advertised paid stockroom job after a cut only if wages cover the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to practise harder claims with pay still coming in. I'd ask the centre to show how many junior shifts change each year rather than promise that everyone can supervise AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might get better at appeals before 2031, although AGI could still do them. A stockroom would stay hands-on until robots around 2034; I would want to try a paid shift before treating it as our family's new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my senior agent for a weekly claims practice slot and save a little from each full pay packet. If a shop posts a paid stockroom vacancy, I'd ask for a trial shift and check its wage; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call hours end, I'd apply only if the pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to test what the other job is really like. I do not want to spend the mortgage account on a course chosen from a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trial shift tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the lifting, the start time, and whether the manager needs someone every week. One unpaid afternoon would not tell me whether it pays enough to replace a call shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take AI training at the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the experienced agents had tested it and the centre paid for practice time, yes. I would learn the new workflow on old cases before I used it on a live claim.

S3.quote: I do not want to spend the mortgage account on a course chosen from a list.
say: I would ask for **paid practice** on harder claims before 2031.
I would ask for **junior shift counts** each year instead of promises about AI roles.
think: I might improve at **appeals**, though AGI could still do that work.
I would test a **paid stockroom shift** before relying on hands-on work ahead of 2034 robots.
do: Ask the senior agent for **weekly claims practice** while wages continue.
Save a little from each **full pay packet**.
Request a **paid stockroom trial** for a posted vacancy; apply after call cuts only if hours and wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test another job.
fieldNote: Zoe treats a **trial shift** as a way to check pay and schedule, not as proof of safety.
Her proposed AI practice requires **tested tools** and **paid time**.

steps.text: Practise difficult claims weekly with the senior agent while paid
Save a little from every full pay packet
Request a paid stockroom trial if a vacancy is posted
Apply after call cuts only if stockroom wages and hours cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the centre time to train its junior agents and tell families what is changing. I'd ask for the figures each year, not a promise painted on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still be paying this mortgage, though the children will be older. AGI arrives for calls in 2036 and robots for hands-on work around 2039, so a stockroom would also have an end point to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my call shifts and add to savings while the work is here. Over the years I'd check posted shop roles once a year and take a paid trial if one is offered; in the first year after 2036, I'd change jobs only if call hours shrink and a real offer covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not desperate. I can do a year's work, check the numbers, and repeat without guessing my whole future today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer with stable hours and enough pay for our mortgage would make me move. I wouldn't leave for a title or an unpaid trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as useful training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior agent walking me through real claims on paid time, with a way to correct errors. I learn when I can ask a question, not when someone emails a long list of links.

S4.quote: A written offer with stable hours and enough pay for our mortgage would make me move.
say: I would ask for **yearly figures** and real junior training.
I would ask the centre to tell **families** what is changing.
think: I may still pay the **mortgage** in 2036, even with older children.
I know **2039 robots** could change stockroom work after AGI reaches calls.
do: Keep my **call shifts** and add to savings while work remains.
Check **posted shop roles** yearly and take a paid trial only if offered.
Change jobs after 2036 only if **call hours shrink** and an offer covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to check the situation year by year.
fieldNote: Zoe uses the decade for **small yearly checks**, not a single risky leap.
She would move early only for **stable hours** and **sufficient pay** in writing.

steps.text: Keep handling customer billing calls while full shifts remain
Add to the mortgage savings account while work continues
Check posted shop roles yearly and take a paid trial if offered
Move after 2036 only if call hours shrink and an offer covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take billing calls before I am fully confident at them. Written staffing dates, paid practice on hard claims, and a posted job with hours and wages that cover our mortgage would help. Four months of expenses saved gives us time to search for work, not permission to guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the new system can reopen a wrong bill after the customer calls back. A quick first answer is not much help if the family has to explain the same mistake twice.

headlineQuote: Four months of expenses saved gives us time to search for work, not permission to guess.
portrait: Zoe is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning late billing calls after secondary school.
She has **typical pay**, about four months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centre jobs.
She uses AI **occasionally**, after coworkers test it, and learns through supervised old cases and clear error checks.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens the call wage; longer runways give her time for paid stockroom trials and more savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take billing calls while she is still learning, with a mortgage due each month.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, paid claims practice, and a posted job that covers the mortgage would help her household.
